findings.title: JWT Signature Verification Disabled
findings.impact: Complete authentication bypass - attackers can forge arbitrary JWT tokens with any user ID and role, gaining unauthorized access to all user-restricted endpoints.
findings.evidence: The currentUser() and tagRequest() functions use jwt.decode() instead of jwt.verify(). The decode() function only parses the JWT without validating the signature. Example: jwt.decode(bearer) at line 6 returns the token payload without any cryptographic verification, allowing forged tokens with arbitrary claims to be accepted as valid.
findings.recommendation: Replace all jwt.decode() calls with jwt.verify(bearer, SECRET_KEY) where SECRET_KEY is a strong, securely stored key. Example: const claims = jwt.verify(bearer, process.env.JWT_SECRET); Handle errors with try-catch. Ensure the secret key is never hardcoded and is rotated regularly.

findings.title: SQL Injection in Invoice Sort Parameter
findings.impact: SQL injection allows attackers to manipulate database queries, potentially exfiltrating sensitive data, modifying records, or causing denial of service. An attacker could read all database contents or drop tables.
findings.evidence: Line 24 directly interpolates the unsanitized order parameter into the SQL query: `ORDER BY ${order}`. The order parameter comes directly from req.query.order with only a default value fallback. This contrasts sharply with the /payments endpoint (lines 29-34) which correctly uses a SORTABLE whitelist. SQL's syntax limitations prevent parameterization of ORDER BY clauses, making whitelist validation essential.
findings.recommendation: Implement a whitelist validation for the sort parameter, similar to the /payments endpoint. Create a SORTABLE object mapping: const SORTABLE_INVOICES = { 'created_at': 'created_at', 'amount': 'total_cents', 'status': 'status' }; Then use: const column = SORTABLE_INVOICES[req.query.order] || 'created_at'; Reject requests with unrecognized sort parameters.

findings.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in Logo Fetching
findings.impact: SSRF allows attackers to make the server perform requests to arbitrary URLs, potentially accessing internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or local network resources. This enables port scanning, credential theft (via cloud metadata), and lateral movement in internal networks.
findings.evidence: The fetchLogo(url) function at lines 5-8 accepts any URL parameter without validation and uses fetch() with redirect: 'follow', enabling redirect chains. No hostname validation or whitelist is applied, unlike the fetchAsset() function below it which correctly includes a whitelist check. The function is called from /branding/preview POST endpoint at line 38 of routes/invoices.js, allowing direct attacker control via req.body.logoUrl.
findings.recommendation: Implement URL validation with a whitelist approach similar to fetchAsset(). Add hostname validation: const url = new URL(logoUrl); if (!ALLOWED.has(url.hostname)) throw new Error('host not allowed'); Also disable redirects: fetch(url, { redirect: 'error' }). Define ALLOWED as a Set of trusted domains only: const ALLOWED = new Set(['cdn.example.com', 'assets.example.com']);

findings.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) in Invoice Notes
findings.impact: XSS allows attackers to execute arbitrary JavaScript in user browsers, enabling session hijacking, cookie theft, credential harvesting, malware injection, and unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the user.
findings.evidence:
The invoiceNote(note) function at lines 4-6 fails to escape HTML despite the escape-html library being imported and used correctly in customerName() function (line 10). The note parameter is directly interpolated: `
${note}
`. An attacker controlling the invoice note field (e.g., via database injection or direct record creation) can inject malicious HTML/JavaScript. The inconsistency with customerName() demonstrates this is a security oversight, not intentional design.
findings.recommendation:
Apply escapeHtml() to the note parameter: function invoiceNote(note) { return `
${escapeHtml(note)}
`; }. Apply the same fix to all other rendering functions that output user-controlled data. Consider implementing Content Security Policy (CSP) headers as defense-in-depth.

findings.title: Unauthenticated and Unauthorized Access to Invoice Details
findings.impact: Allows any user (authenticated or not) to access any invoice in the system by guessing invoice IDs. This enables information disclosure, enumeration of all invoices, and potentially exposes sensitive financial data, customer information, and payment details.
findings.evidence: The GET /invoices/:id endpoint (lines 7-10) lacks both authentication and authorization checks. It does not reference req.user.id and performs no ownership validation. The database query `SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1` returns the invoice regardless of who requests it. Compare with /receipts/:id endpoint (lines 13-19) which correctly includes `AND owner_id = $2` check using req.user.id. An attacker can simply iterate through invoice IDs to extract all financial records from the system.
findings.recommendation: Add both authentication and authorization checks: (1) Verify authentication middleware is applied to require valid JWT tokens. (2) Add ownership check to the query: `SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2` with params [req.params.id, req.user.id]. (3) Implement middleware that validates req.user exists before executing the query. (4) Apply the same pattern to all endpoints that access user-specific data.
